title: She Has Lost Nine Straight Matches Against An Se Young. On Wednesday in Jakarta, Sindhu Will Try Again.
excerpt: PV Sindhu's Indonesia Open run — and her return to the world's top 10 — now runs directly through the most dominant player in women's badminton.
body:
PV Sindhu returned to the world's top 10 this week for the first time since October 2023. It took 954 days. Injuries, inconsistency, questions about whether the two-time Olympic medallist could still compete at the sport's highest level — all of it preceded the number that flickered beside her name in the updated BWF rankings: World No. 10.

On Tuesday, she played like it. At the Istora Senayan in Jakarta — one of badminton's most iconic arenas — Sindhu beat Thailand's Busanan Ongbamrungphan 25-23, 21-16 in the opening round of the Indonesia Open 2026, extending a head-to-head record that now stands at a lopsided 21-1.

The scoreline does not tell the full story. Sindhu had Busanan pinned at 19-14 in the first game before the Thai shuttler reeled off five consecutive points to level at 19-19. The arena sensed trouble. Sindhu did not blink. She closed the game at 25-23 with the composure that has defined her best moments, then carried the momentum into a more controlled second game.

## The Wall That Waits

But the Indonesia Open bracket has a particular cruelty built into Sindhu's draw. With top seed An Se Young dispatching Turkey's Neslihan Arin 21-18, 21-6 in her opening match, the two women are set to meet in the Round of 16.

The head-to-head makes uncomfortable reading for Indian fans: Sindhu trails 0-9. Not a single game won in nine meetings. At the Singapore Open just last week, An Se Young ended Sindhu's run in the quarterfinals. Before that, at the India Open in January, An Se Young won 21-13, 21-11 in a match so one-sided it lasted barely half an hour.

An Se Young, 24, is the reigning Olympic champion and has held the World No. 1 ranking for the better part of two years. Her defensive retrieval is elite, her counterattacking smashes arrive from positions that should not generate power, and her court coverage makes even the most precisely placed drops come back with interest. She is, by some distance, the most complete women's singles player in the sport.

## What Has Changed

And yet Sindhu's form this week suggests something has shifted. Coming off a strong quarterfinal showing at the Singapore Open — where she beat Indonesia's Putri Kusuma Wardani, the World No. 9, on her way through the draw — Sindhu has looked lighter on her feet, sharper in her attacking intent, and more willing to dictate rallies from mid-court rather than defend from the baseline.

Her coach and former doubles great Mathias Boe has focused on reducing the length of rallies, encouraging Sindhu to finish points earlier rather than being drawn into the extended exchanges that tend to favour An Se Young's superior fitness. The strategy showed glimpses of working in Singapore, even if the result did not follow.

The broader context matters, too. Sindhu's return to the top 10 is not a statistical fluke. She has been steadily accumulating ranking points across the 2026 circuit, recovering from the long injury layoff that followed her disappointing exit at the Paris Olympics. The movement that once looked laboured now carries its old fluency. The steep smashes that defined her Olympic silver-medal run in Tokyo are landing with authority again.

## The Diaspora Stakes

For millions of NRI fans who have followed Sindhu's career from the 2016 Rio semifinals onward, Wednesday's match carries the weight of something beyond a second-round result at a Super 1000 tournament. Sindhu, alongside Saina Nehwal before her, remains the most visible Indian presence in an East Asian-dominated sport. Every match against the world's best is an assertion that Indian badminton belongs at the highest table.

The nine consecutive losses to An Se Young are a statistical fact. But sport does not always operate within statistics. Sindhu has beaten world number ones before — she stunned Carolina Marin in the 2019 World Championship final and took down Tai Tzu-ying on the Olympic stage in Tokyo. The question is not whether she is capable of an upset. It is whether her body and her game have recovered enough to sustain the intensity required for 40-plus minutes against the best player on the planet.

## What to Watch

If Sindhu comes out attacking, compresses the rallies, and takes risks at the net, the match will be competitive. If she is pulled into long, defensive exchanges — the pattern that has defined all nine losses — An Se Young's fitness and retrieval will wear her down as they always have.

Either way, Wednesday at the Istora Senayan will tell us something important: whether Sindhu's return to the top 10 is a genuine resurgence, or whether the old ceiling still holds.

The match is scheduled for Day 3 of the Indonesia Open. For Indian fans across the world, it will be worth staying up for.
author: Diaspora Desk
